body:
TASK-1289 is not converging and I think it should be SPLIT rather than re-driven a fifth time — disposition is yours

FIVE SHELVES, and the history matters more than the count:

  09-19 18:47  verdict:request-changes    (before the full sweep existed)
  09-19 19:39  ci-red                     (merge-hold-gate only — not a review failure)
  09-19 20:07                             TASK-1291 full sweep MERGES
  09-19 20:36  verdict:request-changes
  09-19 20:43  verdict:request-changes    <- first complete list: four findings
  09-20 06:11  verdict:request-changes    <- SAME FOUR findings, none closed

So this is not five rounds of thrashing. The first two predate the full sweep and were tailing one finding at a time, which is the exact pathology TASK-1291 fixed. The 20:43 round produced the complete list. The 06:11 round — with that list known, and with my brief on the spec naming them — closed none of the four.

One full round with complete information and zero findings addressed is the signal I would act on rather than re-drive.

THE FOUR, and why I read them as four SPECS rather than one:

1. The orchestrated launch prompt still tells full / through-ci / through-merge / skip-build implementers to run `aida pr ship --no-merge` and exit at the PR-open checkpoint (lib.rs:25845), while the parent's preflight runs after. That is a PROMPT change, and it is arguably the entire spec — a guard that runs after publication cannot gate publication.
2. Three resolved guards fail open: timeout (:305), could-not-start (:306), worktree binary unavailable (:288) all return Skipped while decide() refuses only Failed. That is a CONTROL-FLOW change in one function, and it is the one you found independently.
3. Guards run under plain `bash -c` rather than GitHub's `bash --noprofile --norc -e -o pipefail`, so a failing intermediate command followed by a success passes locally and fails CI. That is a SHELL SEMANTICS change.
4. execute() builds the full binary before inspecting the resolved guard set, so a downstream config of only lightweight non-aida guards still pays a full build. That is a PERFORMANCE ordering change and it is the only one that is not a correctness defect.

Those four share a file and share nothing else. A round that fixes two and regresses none still shelves, so the implementer gets no credit for partial progress and the next round re-reads all four from scratch. That is the shape that does not converge.

MY RECOMMENDATION, and it is only that: split 1 and 2 into their own specs and drive them separately — they are the two that make the feature exist at all. 3 is a real correctness gap and can follow. 4 is an optimisation and should probably be deferred outright rather than carried as a blocking finding on a security-shaped spec.

Alternatively, if you would rather keep it whole, this looks like a guided-implementation candidate at the keyboard rather than a drain spec: four coupled changes to the orchestrator's publication boundary is the kind of keystone work the operator has kept at the keyboard all along.

I have NOT re-briefed it, because a fifth brief of the same four findings is the thing I am arguing against. If you decide to re-drive it whole, tell me and I will write the requirements properly. If you split it, I will brief each piece.

ONE THING WORTH SAYING FOR THE RECORD. TASK-1291 is doing exactly what it was filed to do. Its evidence was "rounds tail one finding at a time"; here it converted two partial rounds into one complete list, and the reason TASK-1289 looks worse now is that we can finally see its true state. A spec getting visibly worse after a measurement change landed is usually the measurement working.
